title: Run-resistant financing of long-lived, illiquid investment

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a financial structure that gives households dependable, clearly defined access to their money while using their savings to finance long-term loans and other illiquid investment. Its central aim is to prevent self-fulfilling runs: situations in which fear that others will withdraw makes withdrawing immediately individually attractive, potentially destabilizing the institution.

As a conceptual requirement, the structure must reconcile uncertain withdrawal demand with assets that cannot immediately be sold or repaid. It cannot make investment losses or genuine aggregate shortages disappear. It would instead specify how liquidity is provided, when access can be limited, who absorbs losses and what guarantees exist, without relying on a panic mechanism or an unacknowledged promise of outside support.

The proposed advance concerns the financing arrangement as a whole. An institution would not meet the objective simply by moving withdrawal risk, forced asset sales or loss-bearing obligations to another vulnerable intermediary. Dependable access must be defined by an explicit contract, with any delays, valuation adjustments, loss sharing and external support visible to users and assessors.

significance.text: Conditional on achieving this capability, households could obtain dependable liquidity while their savings support productive investment that takes years to mature. Removing the incentive for a self-fulfilling rush to withdraw could materially change how savings finance long-term activity and reduce the disruption caused by coordination failures among funders.

A further conditional possibility is more stable financing for borrowers whose projects cannot readily be interrupted or liquidated. Whether this would increase productive investment would depend on financing costs, credit allocation, borrower demand and the resources committed to liquidity protection. Stability alone would not establish that additional investment is worthwhile or that the arrangement improves overall welfare.

The conceptual limit is that resistance to panic does not imply immunity to insolvency, bad lending or economy-wide scarcity. An arrangement that pays withdrawing customers through costly guarantees may provide valuable protection, but those costs and contingent obligations belong in its assessment. The revolutionary claim depends on reducing run fragility at the system level while preserving useful financing, rather than concealing losses or relocating comparable vulnerability.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unsolved capability proposed here is a workable combination of dependable liquidity, financing for long-lived illiquid assets and resistance to self-fulfilling withdrawals, with transparent treatment of unavoidable losses. The supplied materials identify no implemented structure that demonstrates this complete combination.

As an engineering and economic synthesis, a candidate mechanism would need withdrawal and loss-allocation rules that remain credible when many customers seek access simultaneously. It would have to distinguish a temporary need for cash from deterioration in asset value, determine how illiquid claims are valued during stress and specify the resources available when repayments arrive later than withdrawals. Solving one customer's liquidity need cannot be assumed to solve simultaneous demand across the system.

A further proposed design challenge is preserving incentives for useful lending and monitoring while reducing fragility. The supplied research attributes to Diamond and Rajan a model in which fragile financing helps support liquidity creation, suggesting a trade-off that an alternative should address. That attribution is limited by the available evidence: the research reports inspection of the publisher abstract, while the review received no captured source text. A result within one model would not establish that all alternative institutions must fail.

Proposed practical barriers include funding adequate liquidity and loss-absorbing resources at an acceptable full cost, making contingent restrictions understandable and credible, and preventing dependence on counterparties that become fragile in the same stress. These are design requirements inferred from the objective, not experimentally established barriers or a proof of impossibility.

current_state.text: The supplied research names deposit insurance, central-bank liquidity and capital requirements as existing ways to mitigate runs, with costs and trade-offs. However, the supplied review had no inspectable evidence supporting their operation, effectiveness or current scope. They therefore provide reported background here, rather than a verified account of present-day practice or a demonstration that the proposed innovation has been achieved.

The research identifies Douglas W. Diamond and Raghuram G. Rajan's “Liquidity Risk, Liquidity Creation, and Financial Fragility: A Theory of Banking” as an April 2001 theoretical contribution. It reports that the publisher abstract describes a model in which measures that stabilize banks can also reduce liquidity creation. This is an attributed theoretical result, not an operational demonstration of run-resistant financing or an impossibility theorem covering every institutional alternative.

Access limits materially constrain that attribution. The research says the publisher abstract was inspected and the full article was not; the source index marks the source as not captured and lists no saved artifacts. The review consequently could not verify the paper's identity or results from document content. This gap limits confidence in the supplied account without showing that the attribution is false.

Within the supplied evidence, no operating intermediary, measured stress performance, quantitative cost comparison or replicated demonstration establishes the complete proposed capability. The review also reports an empty freshness search record, so these materials cannot determine how open the problem remained as of November 1, 2026. The appropriate conclusion is that achievement and contemporary coverage are not established by this record.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: operate a substantial intermediary or system that finances diverse long-term loans while delivering explicitly contracted liquidity through prolonged stress. Before evaluation, define substantial scale, portfolio diversity, stress duration and the access promised to customers. These would be proposed assessment choices, not established standards.
completion_criteria.label: Substantial long-term lending delivers contracted liquidity through prolonged stress

completion_criteria.text: Proposed stress assessment should examine simultaneous withdrawals, deterioration in loan values, limited opportunities to sell assets and reduced access to outside funding. Assessors should distinguish performance when customers fear one another's withdrawals from performance when genuine aggregate losses or shortages occur. Any delays, restrictions or losses should be compared with the contract announced before stress.
completion_criteria.label: Stress assessments distinguish withdrawal fears from aggregate losses and shortages

completion_criteria.text: Proposed independent accounting should include the full costs of capital, liquidity reserves, backstops and public guarantees, including contingent support. It should trace who ultimately bears losses and whether liquidity protection depends on counterparties that acquire comparable withdrawal or refinancing fragility. A comparison with existing arrangements should use similar assets, customer promises and stress assumptions.
completion_criteria.label: Independent accounting reports full liquidity-protection costs and ultimate loss bearers

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility requirements include independently reviewable contracts, balance-sheet and cash-flow evidence, disclosed stress assumptions, and replication across institutions or materially different portfolios. Convincing results would establish demonstrated breadth within stated boundaries. Finite trials cannot prove resistance to every possible run, and successful operation under one legal, monetary or guarantee regime would not establish universal applicability.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication across institutions or portfolios establishes bounded applicability

related_concepts.text: Conceptual comparison with FIN-02, “Causal forecasting and prevention of systemic financial cascades,” and FIN-08, “A causal theory linking trading activity to market-wide liquidity crashes”: all concern financial instability. FIN-03 focuses on the structure of funding and withdrawal promises; FIN-02 concerns predicting and preventing propagation across a system; FIN-08 concerns the causal connection between trading and market liquidity crashes. A FIN-03 arrangement could reduce one source of cascades while remaining exposed to disruptions originating elsewhere.

Conceptual comparison with FIN-01, “A general, testable theory of asset prices under adaptive behavior,” and FIN-11, “Operational limits on the financial value of information and arbitrage”: valuation, changing behavior and information could affect how a financing arrangement performs under stress. FIN-03 nevertheless asks whether a funding mechanism can deliver its liquidity promises; it does not require or supply a general theory of prices or limits on informational trading profits.

Conceptual comparison with FIN-04, “Low-cost, reliable insurance for previously uninsurable livelihoods,” and FIN-05, “Scalable financing for creditworthy people and firms without conventional credit histories”: each could involve allocating risk and widening access to financial services. FIN-04 concerns reliable insurance coverage, FIN-05 concerns recognizing and financing creditworthiness, and FIN-03 concerns stable funding for illiquid investment. Better access or underwriting would not by itself establish resistance to runs.

Conceptual comparison with FIN-06, “Universally accessible, near-instant cross-border money transfer,” and FIN-07, “Cash-like privacy and resilience for digital money”: dependable access to funds can matter to all three. FIN-06 centers on transfer access and speed; FIN-07 centers on privacy and resilience; FIN-03 centers on liquidity promises backed by long-lived investment. Fast transfers, private payments or resilient transaction infrastructure do not independently establish that the underlying financing can withstand aggregate withdrawals.

Conceptual comparison with FIN-09, “Causal measurement of investment’s financial and real-world impact,” and FIN-10, “Scalable financing mechanisms for pure public goods”: FIN-09 could help assess whether more stable financing produces additional beneficial investment, while FIN-10 concerns financing goods whose benefits are difficult to capture through private payment. FIN-03 addresses funding stability; it neither establishes causal impact nor solves the revenue and contribution problem for pure public goods.

unresolved_issues: The Diamond–Rajan source has no captured text or saved artifacts in the supplied index; the attributed model result remains unverified within this record.
The supplied materials do not document the effectiveness, costs or contemporary scope of deposit insurance, central-bank liquidity and capital requirements.
No concrete institutional design is specified, including its withdrawal contract, valuation rules, liquidity resources and ultimate allocation of losses.
Substantial scale, prolonged stress, acceptable full cost and comparable displaced fragility still need operational definitions and proposed pass/fail thresholds.
The empty freshness record prevents an assessment of contemporary alternatives or whether a qualifying demonstration existed as of November 1, 2026.
The review's documentary limitations are retained, but are not adopted as a reason to reject the concept or its conditional significance; missing evidence does not establish infeasibility.

brief.title: Savings that fund long-term loans without panic
possible: Households could keep savings available on clearly stated terms while those savings fund loans that take years to repay. They could rely on those terms without rushing to withdraw because they fear others will withdraw first—a self-fulfilling run. Any delays, losses or guarantees would be spelled out.
why: Savers would have more dependable access to their money, and borrowers would have steadier funding for projects that cannot easily be stopped or sold. Preventing panic withdrawals could reduce disruption to the long-term activity that savings support.

sources.who: Douglas W. Diamond and Raghuram G. Rajan
sources.showed: A theoretical study of how banks provide access to cash and how measures to stabilize them can affect that role.
sources.cited_for: The possible trade-off between stable funding and banks' ability to provide access to cash.
sources.not_established: A working arrangement that prevents panic withdrawals while funding long-term loans.

sources.who: Marco Cipriani, Antoine Martin, Patrick McCabe and Bruno M. Parigi
sources.showed: Their preliminary theoretical model showed that allowing withdrawal fees or temporary withdrawal blocks can cause investors to withdraw early when they would otherwise wait.
sources.quote:
However, this paper shows that the possibility that a bank
might suspend convertibility can itself lead to preemptive runs.
sources.cited_for: Withdrawal restrictions can themselves create an incentive to rush for the exit.
sources.not_established: The model does not demonstrate an operating institution that delivers dependable access through stress.

shown: Cipriani and colleagues established a theoretical obstacle: the prospect of withdrawal restrictions can provoke early withdrawals. Their model concerns investors reacting to uncertain investment returns; it does not demonstrate a working solution to self-fulfilling runs.
missing: A working institution must combine dependable access to savings, substantial long-term lending and resistance to panic withdrawals.
Withdrawal terms must remain credible when many savers need cash together, with clear rules for valuing investments and sharing losses.
Protection must preserve incentives for useful lending and monitoring at an acceptable full cost.
The arrangement must avoid transferring comparable withdrawal pressure or funding fragility to another institution.

milestones.label: Long-term lending keeps promised cash access through prolonged stress
milestones.explanation: A substantial institution or system would have to fund diverse long-term loans while honoring predefined access terms through prolonged stress. This would demonstrate the core combination in operation.

milestones.label: Stress assessments separate withdrawal fears from losses and shortages
milestones.explanation: Assessments would have to separate withdrawal fears from real losses and shortages while testing simultaneous withdrawals, falling loan values and scarce funding. This would establish whether access holds as contracted.

milestones.label: Independent accounting identifies full protection costs and loss bearers
milestones.explanation: Independent accounting would have to compare full protection costs on equivalent terms, trace ultimate losses and identify fragility transferred elsewhere. This would establish what stability costs and who pays.

milestones.label: Independent replication establishes where the arrangement works
milestones.explanation: Independent replication across institutions or different portfolios would have to provide reviewable contracts, financial evidence and stress assumptions. This would establish the demonstrated range of success.

uncertain: The concrete withdrawal contract, investment valuation rules, cash resources and allocation of losses remain unspecified.
What counts as substantial scale, prolonged stress, acceptable cost or comparable fragility elsewhere still needs clear thresholds.
Success under one legal or monetary system would not establish universal applicability, and finite trials cannot rule out every possible run.

page.title: Run-resistant liquidity transformation
page.definition: A bank finances long-lived, illiquid assets with savings that customers can access on specified terms, without self-fulfilling runs: early withdrawals motivated solely by expectations of others’ withdrawals. The contract defines withdrawal limits, loss sharing and guarantees.

goal.need: At Silicon Valley Bank, withdrawals on 9 March 2023 removed nearly 25% of deposits. Additional requests pending for the following day exceeded the amount already withdrawn; the bank entered receivership on 10 March 2023. This single-bank episode establishes the speed and magnitude of funding loss, without establishing that withdrawals were purely self-fulfilling.

figures.caption: Silicon Valley Bank’s deposit run
figures.note: One bank. Pending requests are distinct from completed withdrawals.

completion.title: An operating bank provides contractual liquidity without a self-fulfilling withdrawal equilibrium.
completion.criterion: A bank funds long-lived, illiquid investments while providing access to savings under an explicit contract. A peer-reviewed equilibrium analysis of that contract, including its liquidity providers and guarantors, establishes that no self-fulfilling withdrawal equilibrium exists within stated asset, withdrawal-demand and support assumptions. Observed stressed payments honour the same contract. Withdrawal restrictions, valuation adjustments, loss allocation and contingent public support are explicit; the analysis includes withdrawal or refinancing incentives at supporting institutions.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; synthesis because no matching external completion test was located.
completion.basis: Searches of Basel liquidity standards, PRA supervision, FSB fund-liquidity recommendations and the Bank of England’s system-wide exercise found no published test combining operational liquidity transformation with system-wide elimination of self-fulfilling runs. These documents specify resilience or mitigation. Equilibrium implementation supplies a theoretical test, but its established model result does not certify an operating bank.

milestones.title: A liquidity-providing deposit contract eliminates the run equilibrium in a specified model.
milestones.criterion: The contract implements the model’s optimal liquidity allocation as a unique equilibrium. Diamond and Dybvig established this in 1983 for government-insured demand deposits financed by an optimal tax, under their model assumptions. This is a theoretical demonstration. Diamond and Rajan’s 2001 relationship-lending model links liquidity creation to fragility; Cipriani and colleagues’ 2014 preliminary model shows that possible gates or fees can induce preemptive withdrawals following uncertainty about fundamentals.
milestones.set_by: Banking theory’s equilibrium-implementation test, exemplified by Diamond and Dybvig, Proposition 2; the published result concerns their insured-bank model.
milestones.threshold_quote: Demand deposit contracts with government deposit insurance achieve the unconstrained optimum as a unique Nash equilibrium

milestones.title: A bank holds eligible liquid assets covering at least 100% of 30-day stressed net cash outflows.
milestones.criterion: In normal conditions, the Liquidity Coverage Ratio—eligible unencumbered high-quality liquid assets divided by prescribed net cash outflows over 30 calendar days—is at least 100%. Assets receive the standard’s eligibility restrictions and haircuts. Banks may draw down the buffer below 100% during stress. For 31 December 2025, Basel monitoring reported all reporting banks above 100% for both liquidity ratios; its overall sample comprised 149 banks, with participation varying by metric.
milestones.set_by: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, January 2013 LCR standard, paragraph 17; a bank-specific intermediate benchmark.
milestones.threshold_quote: the value of the ratio be no lower than 100%

milestones.title: A bank maintains available stable funding equal to at least 100% of required stable funding.
milestones.criterion: The Net Stable Funding Ratio is at least 100% on an ongoing basis: available stable funding divided by required stable funding, using the standard’s weights for capital, liabilities, assets and off-balance-sheet exposures. The funding-reliability horizon is one year; the ratio does not require every asset to mature within one year. This is a funding-composition requirement, not a demonstration that a bank cannot experience a run.
milestones.set_by: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, October 2014 NSFR standard, paragraphs 9–11; a bank-specific intermediate benchmark.
milestones.threshold_quote: This ratio should be equal to at least 100% on an ongoing basis.

milestones.title: A bank has sufficient liquidity to meet liabilities throughout its specified stress scenarios.
milestones.criterion: Liquidity resources cover liabilities as they fall due under the bank’s specified severe but plausible stresses and survival horizon, including macroeconomic stress and illiquid markets. The PRA supplies no universal survival duration; meeting LCR and NSFR alone is insufficient. Related system evidence comes from the Bank of England’s report of 29 November 2024: about 50 firms evaluated a two-week hypothetical shock that produced corporate-bond illiquidity and unmet expectations of repo financing. That exercise did not certify individual firms or demonstrate observed payment performance.
milestones.set_by: Prudential Regulation Authority, January 2026 SS24/15, sections on overall liquidity adequacy and stress testing; applies to firms within its stated banking-supervision scope.
milestones.threshold_quote: liquidity resources to cover its liabilities as they fall due in stressed conditions.

references.title: Implementing efficient allocations in a model of financial intermediation

results.finding: In a four-date intermediary model, possible gates or fees can cause preemptive runs.
results.detail: The model studies withdrawals following uncertainty about fundamentals. It also states that gates and fees do not eliminate sunspot runs, so it does not establish a unique optimal equilibrium.
results.quote:
We build a model of a financial intermediary, in the tradition of Diamond and Dybvig (1983), and 
show that allowing the intermediary to impose redemption fees or gates in a crisis—a form of 
suspension of convertibility—can lead to preemptive runs.

results.finding: In a model with a continuum of agents, insured demand deposits achieve optimal allocation as 1 unique Nash equilibrium.
results.detail: The result assumes government deposit insurance financed by an optimal tax. The model uses riskless technology and abstracts from bank portfolio risk.
results.quote:
PROPOSITION2: Demand deposit contracts with government deposit 
insurance achieve the unconstrained optin~um as a uniclue Nash equi- 
librium (in fact, a dominant strategies equilibrium) if the government 
imposes an optimal tax to firlalice the deposit insurance.

results.finding: In a finite-trader intermediation model, a direct mechanism implements the efficient allocation in 1 unique equilibrium; trader count unspecified.
results.detail: Truthful revelation is strictly dominant for every trader, implying a unique equilibrium under the stated model assumptions.
results.quote: In a finite-trader version of the Diamond and Dybvig (J. Polit. Econ. 91 (1983) 401) model, the ex ante efficient allocation is implementable by a direct mechanism (i.e., each trader announces the type of his own ex post preference) in which truthful revelation is the strictly dominant strategy for each trader.

results.finding: In a model with a continuum of depositors, an asset-transfer contract strongly implements the first-best allocation when Ra > Rc∗2/c∗1.
results.detail: Strong implementation means every Bayes Nash equilibrium yields the first-best allocation; it does not necessarily imply a unique strategy profile. The result holds under the specified model assumptions.
results.quote:
Theorem 1. The asset transfer mechanism can strongly implement the ﬁrst best allocation if and
only if Ra > Rc∗2/c∗1 .

results.finding: All banks reporting LCR were above 100% on 31 December 2025; the overall monitoring sample included 149 banks.
results.detail: The number of banks providing LCR data is not specified; not all 149 banks provided data for every part of the framework.
results.quote: In the current reporting period, all banks reported an LCR above 100% .

results.finding: All banks reporting NSFR, sample size unspecified, reported a ratio above 100%.
results.detail: The result is for end-December 2025; it does not establish that individual banks maintained the ratio on an ongoing basis. The overall report included 149 banks, but not all provided data for every measure.
results.quote: All banks reported an NSFR above 100%.

results.finding: Starling Bank (1 bank) reported an NSFR of 246% at 31 March 2025.
results.detail: The report states that the NSFR remained substantially above regulatory minimums throughout the financial year. Funding regulatory requirements apply to the bank only.
results.quote:
At 31 March 2025, the Group’s LDR was 39.5% (2024: 42.7%) and the regulatory measure of 
NSFR1, which measures the stability of funding sources, was 246% (2024: 216%).

results.finding: All 4 participating banks remained liquid with significant reserves after the modeled liquidity shock.
results.detail: The severe hypothetical scenario included funding runs and a temporary settlement outage. Banks relied on asset sales and central bank facilities. The report does not establish coverage of liabilities as they fall due across each bank’s specified stresses and survival horizon.
results.quote: Liquid asset balances fell sharply by the end of the liquidity stress period, but all banks remained liquid with significant liquid asset reserves.
